name: Hawaii
summary_text: Visitors to Hawaii stand under the United States federal framework. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, defines sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary; the State Department stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted, and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed the changed treatment to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.  Document risk is documented rather than theoretical. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records. A separate exposure attaches at visa stage: the State Department announced on 5 February 2025 that trans athletes would be barred from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, applicants who list a gender other than their sex assigned at birth are treated as grounds for a permanent ban on fraud grounds, and flagged applications carry an internal marking.  State-level conditions in Hawaii sit at the protective end of the national range. A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and withdrawal of legal recognition, places Hawaii among fifteen states in the Most Protective tier, describing their laws as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.  Hawaii also operates a healthcare shield, listed on the Movement Advancement Project Transgender Healthcare Equality Map with data current to 27 September 2026 as a state holding a shield law or executive order in 2026. The shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where the care is legal in Hawaii but banned in the patient's home state, which makes Hawaii directly usable as a care destination by visitors travelling from prohibiting jurisdictions. The same map counts 16 states and the District of Columbia holding shields, covering 38% of trans people aged 13 and over, against 32 states and 5 territories, 56%, holding none.

name: Idaho
summary_text: A trans visitor to Idaho stands under the United States federal framework in every respect concerning documents and entry. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the changed treatment of trans passports to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.  Idaho's own statute is the sharper exposure on the ground. House Bill 752 was signed by the governor and takes effect on 1 July 2026. It makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room that does not match their sex in government buildings and in public-facing private businesses, including gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues and hospitals. A first offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to a year in jail.  According to the ACLU, House Bill 752 is the only state law in the country extending bathroom criminalisation to private businesses, and it carries steeper penalties than other states' bans. Six transgender Idahoans filed suit on 30 April 2026, before the 1 July effect date, arguing that the measure is unconstitutional. The ACLU's filing asserts due-process, equal-protection and privacy violations and notes that the law targets no actual criminal conduct. National wire reporting covered the legislature's passage of the ban and the jail penalties it carries, along with a lawsuit that has partially blocked it.  A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.
